clinicalPearls: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in appearance that are unobservable or appear only slight to others, causing marked distress or impairment.
Classified within the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders spectrum.
Repetitive behaviours such as mirror-checking or avoidance, grooming, skin-picking, reassurance-seeking, and comparing, or mental acts, occur in response to appearance concerns.
Common foci are the skin, hair, nose, and other facial features; muscle dysmorphia, a preoccupation with insufficient muscularity, is a recognised specifier.
High rates of depression and social anxiety accompany notably high suicidality, which is a leading clinical concern.
Frequently presents to dermatology, cosmetic, and maxillofacial or plastic surgery services rather than psychiatry, and cosmetic procedures rarely satisfy and may worsen the condition.
Insight is often poor and may reach delusional intensity as a specifier, yet the condition still responds to serotonergic and cognitive-behavioural treatment.

First-line management combines serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often requiring higher-range dosing and prolonged trials, with cognitive-behavioural therapy incorporating exposure and response prevention.
reference.pathophysiology: Body dysmorphic disorder shares mechanisms with obsessive-compulsive disorder, involving fronto-striatal and limbic circuitry and serotonergic dysfunction. Patients show abnormal visual processing biased toward detailed, piecemeal analysis of appearance rather than global or holistic processing, with heightened activity in visual and orbitofrontal-striatal systems. Cognitive-behavioural models emphasise selective attention to perceived flaws, distorted self-image, maladaptive appearance-related beliefs, and safety and checking behaviours that maintain distress. Emotional processing biases, such as interpreting neutral facial expressions as contemptuous, reinforce social anxiety and avoidance.
additionalDifferentials: Eating disorders where the concern is weight or shape
Gender dysphoria where distress concerns sex characteristics
Normal appearance concern or actual disfigurement
additionalInvestigations: Structured assessment such as the BDD-YBOCS and validated screening questions
Suicide risk assessment, which is essential
Screening for depression, social anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and eating disorder
History of cosmetic or dermatological procedures sought or undergone
Collateral history regarding functioning and behaviours
redFlags: Active suicidal ideation or previous attempts, indicating high risk
Escalating pursuit of cosmetic surgery or self-performed procedures
Severe social isolation and functional collapse
Skin-picking causing tissue damage or infection
reference.prognosis: Without treatment the disorder tends to be chronic; with adequate-dose serotonergic medication and cognitive-behavioural therapy many patients improve substantially, though relapse can occur if treatment is stopped prematurely.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis behind depression, social anxiety, or repeated cosmetic requests
Endorsing or facilitating cosmetic procedures that typically fail to help
Under-dosing or curtailing serotonergic trials and omitting exposure-based cognitive-behavioural therapy
references: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry
NICE guidance on obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder
management: Serotonergic antidepressants (SSRIs), typically at the higher end of dosing and for an adequate duration, as first-line pharmacotherapy
Cognitive-behavioural therapy tailored to the disorder, incorporating exposure and response prevention and cognitive work on appearance-related beliefs
Structured suicide risk assessment with a crisis and safety plan, given the high suicidality
Counsel against cosmetic, dermatological and surgical procedures, which rarely satisfy and may worsen the condition
Identify and treat comorbid depression, social anxiety and substance use, augmenting with an antipsychotic in refractory or delusional cases
Psychiatric referral and consideration of more intensive or inpatient care when risk is high, with relapse prevention as medication is continued
